agent_notes: Whether vv.6-19 are the psalmist's own imprecation or the enemies' curse that he quotes (so that v.20 answers it) is disputed; the commentaries in the packet read them as his curse, Malbim as the curse his enemies laid on him turned back on them. I translated the Hebrew as it stands and did not adjudicate.

The verbs of vv.17-19 are past-tense narrative forms (wayyiqtol), not jussives. KJV, Webster and BBE turn them into wishes ('so let it come'); ASV and YLT keep the past. I kept the past in the literal layer and the dramatic layer; Radak and Meiri read the past as a prophetic perfect for the future, which I give in the commentary.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses chalal as 'someone has pierced'; the form is a stative perfect (pointed unusually, half qamets, half patach, as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri note), so I glossed it 'is pierced'.
The preposition min in mi-shamen can mean 'from fatness' (lost fat) or 'for lack of oil/fat'; I took it as the first. The English versions agree on 'fatness' except BBE.

The Hebrew has a participle-less imperfect 'they see me' followed directly by 'they shake': a sequence without 'when'. I kept it paratactic in the literal layer and supplied 'when' only in the dramatic layer, where the KJV and ASV also supply it.
Final -āh on 'asitāh is the 3fs suffix 'it'. Meiri reads it as a mappiq he standing for 'asita otah; I follow the plain suffix reading.

'qamu vayyevoshu' is a perfect followed by a wayyiqtol, which can be a prophetic perfect or a wish. The five English versions split (KJV/ASV as jussive, YLT as plain statement, BBE as petition). Meiri on Psalm 109:28 takes the perfect as standing for the future. I rendered it as a certainty in the literal layer ('they have arisen and they are ashamed') and as a confident assertion in the dramatic layer.

agent_notes: The Targum has 'among the wise' for 'rabbim', which differs from the Hebrew 'many'. I follow the Hebrew.

'mishoftei nafsho' is literally 'from the judges of his life/soul'. The KJV 'condemn' and BBE 'go after his soul' interpret; Malbim reads a literal court setting. I kept 'judges' in the literal layer and left the court reading open in the dramatic layer.
STEPBible glosses 'va'ani tefillah' as '[am] prayer'; I kept the verbless Hebrew 'and I - prayer' in the literal layer and unpacked it in the dramatic layer.

The speaker of vv.6-19 is disputed. Most English versions read them as David's imprecations; others (and Radak's note on the singular 'him') take them as the enemies' words quoted against David, opening after the plural 'they' of vv.2-5 and closing before v.20 ('This is the reward of my accusers'). The singular 'him' after plural enemies is the pressure point. Both literal and dramatic layers keep the verbs as jussive wishes, without choosing a speaker; the commentary mentions the option.

STEPBible tags satan as deity.satan. Here haSatan has no article and works as a common noun, 'an accuser/adversary' (cf. v.4 yistenuni, v.20, v.29, and 1 Kgs 11:14, where 'a satan' is a human rival). I glossed it 'an accuser' and kept 'Satan' out of the dramatic layer.
